Are You Exploring All Your Career in Design Options?

It’s surprising how many students believe that NID NIFT & UCEED are the only pathways into design.

The reality? Design education in India offers multiple entrance exams and universities, each with its own strengths, specialisations and opportunities. Yet many students never learn about these options because they are only guided toward the most commonly known exams or given options with hefty fee structure. 

Every student is different. Some may thrive in product design, others in communication design, animation, fashion, architecture, UX, game design or strategic design. The best college is not always the most famous one, it’s the one that aligns with your skills, interests and career goals.

featured_reviews.name: Dr. Aman Bhonsle
featured_reviews.review_text:
I’ve spent a decade in Southeast Asia. I’ve seen how cultural centres work there. Not just as venues, but as ecosystems. Programming, audiences, and moderation move together. Momentum is built deliberately.

In that context, this space feels timely. Important, even.

So I walked into this short film event with my wife. Hopeful.

And credit where it’s due. The space is beautifully put together. Thoughtful. Inviting. Clearly built by people who care. The audience was tuned in.

All the right ingredients were there.

Where the evening struggled was in the films.

Several of the works felt giddy and amateur. Technically rough. Narratively unfocused. Distractingly underdeveloped.

One film had incoherent audio. Meaning became guesswork, not interpretation.

Another leaned hard into abstraction. Not out of necessity. More like a shortcut. It tried, sheepishly, to channel Lynch or Nolan but landed closer to a junky home video.

Abstraction isn’t the problem. Effort is effort.

Not every film needs to be “Inception”.

But abstraction without craft, clarity, or purpose turns into obfuscation.

The stories strained for depth instead of arriving at it. The result wasn’t mystery. It was work that felt unfinished and flat.

This isn’t the venue’s fault.

But programming work of this quality undermines both the space and the audience who has paid money to be there.

Then came the Q&A.
This is where things felt uncomfortable for me.

One filmmaker seemed drunk on his own mythology. Cocky. Dismissive. Actively discouraging questions. He spoke as if the audience owed him their attention. No respect for their presence or participation. A bad attitude. Plain and simple. He talked about not wanting to make the film. About being drunk through the conception and writing process. No self-awareness. No sense that he was poisoning the room.

It left a sour taste. Which is a shame.

A space this carefully crafted deserves better stewardship of its conversations.

Another film’s “representative” wasn’t even a filmmaker. It was a producer. Someone who hadn’t been at the shoot. Didn’t understand the technical process. Couldn’t answer basic questions.

Why seat someone like that for a Q&A?

The engagement collapsed. Limp. Unsatisfying.

I come from filmmaking and television. I expected some juice.

Back-and-forth.
War stories.
Love of the craft.
Obsession.

Instead, the interactions felt evasive. Hollow. And the films, frankly, had the roughness of poorly made student projects. Which is wild, considering how sharp even simple YouTube and Instagram reels look today.

You can’t blame everything on the venue.
But curation matters. A lot.

Not all events are created equal.

Their Instagram shows a genuine celebration of life and creativity. That’s why I’m willing to believe this was a one-off misstep. Still, it was our first experience of the space.

There were smaller issues too.

The welcome could’ve been warmer. If there’s an event, don’t leave people outside like they’re waiting for a bus. A few extra chairs wouldn’t hurt.

No water. No tea. No snacks.

An odd hosting choice—though the upcoming café sounds promising.

This is a new space. It’s finding its footing.

What’s already been built is impressive.
The foundation is solid.

The trajectory is familiar to me as I’ve watched cultural districts in Osaka, Spain, Taipei, Thailand, Seoul and Singapore flourish during my visits there.

Early experimentation.
Then sharper programming.
Then confidence.

That’s the game.

I’ll return eventually.

This first visit had gaps.
But it also showed promise.

With tighter curation, stronger moderation and better audience care, this space could become a genuine cultural anchor for the city.

featured_reviews.name: Smitha Harish
featured_reviews.review_text:
Best place for learning Indian folk art
I recently took an art course with rooftop, and I must say that it was an excellent experience. Over the course of last few weeks, we covered a variety of folk artforms, such as Madhubani, Warli, Kerala Mural, Aippan art forms etc

What I appreciated most about the course was the teaching style. The artists are very patient, encouraging, and always willing to answer our questions. They also provided us with helpful feedback on our artwork, pointing out areas for improvement while also highlighting what we were doing well.

The sessions were also well-organized and easy to follow. Each week, we received a new art theme to learn, like Lord Ganesha, Maa durga, Peacock art etc which allowed us to learn at our own pace and review as needed.

Overall, I highly recommend this course to anyone interested in learning the basics of Indian folk art.

featured_reviews.name: Nishita Karkera
featured_reviews.review_text: I got to know about Art off belly dance with Sanjana from a friend.. who has been a previous student and now an instructor with her. I wanted to learn this dance form ever since .. and I don’t think I could’ve landed myself at a better place . Be it the techniques or the small nuances of the dance form... they make sure they teach you every small detail with a lot of love passion and expertise. ‘Belly dance with Sanjana’ has been my Saturday afternoon routine since quite some time now... and I can’t wait to go back at it. Also... since the nation wide lock down.. they have been conducting regular online sessions from beginners to advance ... which is commendable. Highly recommend this place for anyone looking at learning belly dance !

featured_reviews.name: Rashmi Oak
featured_reviews.review_text: I came to know about Sanjana’s classes through Instagram and I was so happy to finally have found someone who teaches belly dancing. So far our classes have been taken by Sanjana and Antra. Even though i attend zoom classes, I get the exact same vibe of in person learning. So far I have enjoyed all my 13 classes and I am excited to learn more and more from them. Both of them are excellent instructors and they do have different style of teaching and I equally enjoy learning from both of them. The classes have quite a bit of work with variations of basic steps and practicing them over and over again. It doesn’t matter whether you have a big or a flat belly, you can dance or not, you are thin or big, if you are sincere about the dance form and the learning process, this is THE place for you. Kudos to Sanjana for conducting these sessions👏.

featured_reviews.name: Akanksha Mathur
featured_reviews.review_text: Belly-Dancing isn't easy but Sanjana does just the opposite! If you plan to learn BellyDance, this is the place!
